title: Already, now, going to, not yet
goal: Place events in time without changing a single letter of the verb — using four little markers that work like "already, in the middle of, going to, not yet".
bekal: answer an "already?" question correctly — including when you must say *durung*, not *ora*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Wis mangan durung?
dialogs.intro: Early evening on the boarding-house porch. Pak Broto walks past and greets Dian with a question that in Java works as a greeting, not a real question. Dian answers in krama; then Rini arrives and the talk drops to ngoko.

lines.speaker: Pak Broto:
lines.id: Mbak Dian, have you eaten yet?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Dèrèng, Pak. Nembé badhé mangkat pados nedhan.
lines.id: Not yet, sir. I'm just about to go and find something to eat.
lines.literal: not-yet, Sir. just will set-off look-for food.

lines.speaker: Pak Broto:
lines.text: O, nggih. Warungipun Bu Sri sampun bikak kok.
lines.id: Oh, right. Bu Sri's stall is already open, you know.
lines.literal: oh, yes. stall-of Mrs Sri already open you-know.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.id: Yan! Where are you off to?

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.id: Not yet. I'm waiting for my parcel.

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.text: Ora ngerti. Ket mau durung ana kabar.
lines.id: No idea. There's been no news since earlier.
lines.literal: not know. since earlier not-yet there-is news.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Wis, mangan dhisik waé. Kowé wis tau mangan ing warungé Bu Sri?
lines.id: Oh, never mind — eat first. Have you ever eaten at Bu Sri's stall?
lines.literal: enough, eat first just. you already ever eat at stall-of Mrs Sri?

lines.speaker: Rini:
lines.id: Never. Come on, let's go now.

notes: **Sampun dhahar dèrèng?** is a greeting, not an invitation to dinner. An honest answer — *sampun* (yes) or *dèrèng* (not yet) — is all that's needed. You don't have to say what you ate.

**Notice Pak Broto uses *dhahar*, not *nedha***. He's talking about **Dian's** action, and raising the person you speak to is ordinary courtesy. Dian answers with *mangan* — for her own action she must never raise herself.
**Nembé** (krama) / **lagi** (ngoko) has two close but different meanings: "in the middle of" (*lagi mangan* — eating right now) and "just" (*lagi teka* — just arrived). Context tells them apart.
**Pados** is the krama of *golèk* (to look for). *Golèk* also means "puppet" in *wayang golèk* (wooden puppet theater) — and they really are the same word.
**Dhisik** means "first" (before something else), not "in the old days". *Mangan dhisik* = eat first. For "in the old days" use *biyèn*. Krama for *dhisik* is *rumiyin*.
**Ayo** is the ngoko "come on, let's"; krama *mangga*. More urgent: *ayo ta!* or *ayo gek!*

grammars.title: Four markers, and a verb that never moves
body: All these markers stand **in front of** the verb, and the verb itself doesn't change at all — no *-ed*, no *-ing*, no *will*. All you need is the vocabulary.
after: **Durung is not ora.** This is the most common beginner's mistake. *Aku ora mangan* means I'm not eating, full stop (maybe fasting, maybe not hungry); *aku durung mangan* means I haven't eaten yet but will.
**To answer a "wis … durung?" question**, one word is enough: *wis* or *durung*. Answering *ora* sounds wrong and a little curt.
**Wis also means "enough, never mind"** when it opens a sentence to wrap something up: *wis, mangan dhisik waé* (never mind, just eat first). You'll hear it constantly.

Short answer
rows: Have you ever been to Solo?

blocks.title: Why Javanese people always ask "have you eaten?"
items: The question is a sign of care — not empty small talk and not an invitation. It shows the other person treats you as someone whose well-being is worth asking about.
The safest reply: **honest, short, then return it**. *Dèrèng, Pak. Panjenengan sampun?* — Not yet, sir. Have you?
If you say *dèrèng* in someone's home, you'll very likely be served food. It isn't a trap; that's how it works. If you don't want to eat, say *sampun, matur nuwun* (I have, thank you).

blocks.text: You now have enough to build complete sentences. The order is the same as in English — doer, marker, verb, object, extras:

**Time expressions can move to the front** for emphasis, just as in English: *sésuk aku arep nyang pasar* and *aku arep nyang pasar sésuk* are both correct. What can't move is the marker-then-verb order.

Meaning
rows: will not — rare; *ora bakal* is more usual

blocks.text: **Mèh** (almost) is very useful and easily forgotten: *mèh tekan* (almost there), *mèh rampung* (almost done), *mèh waé tiba* (very nearly fell). Krama is *ambèng*, or more often *mèh* too.
